description: We are Team BlackBox — builders of IGNIS, our NASA Space Apps 2026 project harmonizing NASA's split MODIS + VIIRS fire record into a 26-year early-warning calendar. Skills: full-stack web (Next.js/TypeScript), geospatial mapping (MapLibre, GIBS), ML (scikit-learn, models on Hugging Face), open-data pipelines. We love Earth observation, open science and shipping real products. Join us to turn NASA data into impact. Looking for: UI/UX design, geospatial analysis, DevOps, science communication.
summary: IGNIS turns NASA's split fire record into one continuous 26-year Burning Activity Calendar (2000 → today) and a live early-warning platform. MODIS (1 km, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) detect the same landscape very differently, so the two eras cannot be compared without harmonization. IGNIS precomputed a harmonized, calibrated calendar for 9 regions + Bangladesh from the GIBS archive, fuses it with live 5-sensor FIRMS hotspots, and layers early warning on top: DBSCAN segmentation into classified fire boundaries (MEGAFIRE / ESTABLISHED / EMERGING / SCATTERED), persistent fire-system tracking across a 7-day replay, daily dynamics with MODIS↔VIIRS cross-validation, robust trend and seasonal outlooks, fire-weather fusion, and a grounded AI Analyst that writes incident-style situation reports strictly from live telemetry, with deterministic offline fallbacks. It matters because it closes the sensor-era gap, shifts response from snapshot detection to days-ahead warning, and is fully open: free in the browser, runnable on low-end hardware via a GPU-free dual renderer, with four trained models and the 26-year dataset open-sourced on Hugging Face.
details:
What it does / how it works.
IGNIS unifies NASA's split fire record into one continuous 26-year Burning Activity Calendar (2000 → today) and turns it into early warning. MODIS (1 km, Terra 2000 + Aqua 2002) and VIIRS (375 m, S-NPP 2012, NOAA-20 2018, NOAA-21 2023) detect the same landscape very differently — a fire VIIRS sees can be invisible to MODIS — so the two eras can't be compared without harmonization. IGNIS precomputed that harmonized calendar for 9 regions + Bangladesh from the GIBS archive, fuses it with live 5-sensor FIRMS hotspots, segments detections in-browser (DBSCAN + convex-hull boundaries) into classified fire clusters (MEGAFIRE / ESTABLISHED / EMERGING / SCATTERED), tracks persistent fire systems across a 7-day replay, and adds daily dynamics with MODIS↔VIIRS cross-validation, robust trend analysis (Theil-Sen, CUSUM, STL), harmonic-regression seasonal outlooks, fire-weather fusion, and a grounded AI Analyst that writes incident-style situation reports strictly from live telemetry.

Benefits.
It is free, browser-based, and needs no data-science skills: anyone can open it and read 26 years of fire history or today's fire behavior in seconds. It works even where the primary FIRMS API is blocked, thanks to a GIBS vector-tile fallback, and it runs on ordinary laptops via a GPU-free dual map renderer. Every panel discloses its data source, pipeline note and uncertainty — users see how much to trust what they see. The calendar dataset and four trained models are open-sourced, so agencies and researchers can build on it directly.

Intended impact.
Close the sensor-era gap so long-term fire-activity analysis finally becomes possible; shift response from snapshot detection toward days-ahead early warning; and democratize access — fire managers, disaster agencies, researchers and fire-prone communities (like Bangladesh's Boro rice-residue belt in our home-region spotlight) get decision-grade information without expensive infrastructure. The open models and dataset make IGNIS a foundation others can extend globally.

Tools, languages, hardware, software.
Next.js 16 (App Router), React, TypeScript (strict), Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui, MapLibre GL JS with a Leaflet GPU-free fallback renderer, Three.js, Recharts, transformers.js (ONNX) for in-browser MiniLM; Python + scikit-learn for model training; Llama-3.1-8B via the Hugging Face Inference Router for the runtime analyst. No special hardware — ordinary laptops and free tiers (GitHub, Vercel, Hugging Face) plus free NASA APIs (FIRMS MAP_KEY, GIBS, EONET, Earthdata Login). AI-assisted development (z.ai GLM agent) was disclosed and team-verified.

Creativity.
We harmonized first and built features second: the calendar, not a point cloud, is the core artifact. Honesty is part of the interface — continuity coefficients, R², vector-lag notes live on the panels themselves. AI is grounded-only (it may cite telemetry, nothing else) with a deterministic offline fallback producing the same SITREP. ML runs in the user's browser, not on a server. We turned raw detections into actual fire boundaries with advancing-front geometry, and made the record's own flaws visible.

Factors the team considered.
The scale/era mismatch between sensors (we compute and display a continuity coefficient with its CV rather than hiding it); data latency and gaps (GIBS vector lag is disclosed); graceful degradation when upstream APIs fail; accessibility on low-end hardware and weak connections; AI safety (zero-hallucination guard, rule-engine fallback); open licensing (MIT, open weights); credential hygiene; and regional relevance — validating the whole pipeline against the real NASA record for Bangladesh's fire season.
dataRefs: NASA EONET v3 (Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker)
